race_context: The district: East Gibson School Corporation covers Barton, Center and Columbia townships in eastern Gibson County, including Oakland City, Francisco, Mackey, Somerville and Buckskin {wiki_eg}. It now operates Wood Memorial Primary, Wood Memorial Intermediate, Wood Memorial Middle and Wood Memorial High schools, with its central office in Oakland City {eg_site}. Enrollment was 653 in October 2025 and 641 in January 2026, and the district projected 645 students for 2026–27 {pdc_state}{pdc_facilities}. Dr. Michael Galvin has been superintendent since 2024; the board gave him a two-year contract through June 2028 in July 2026 {wfie_galvin}{pdc_textbook}.

The board has five members: Steve Sevier (president), Josh Brewer (vice president), Lynn Rowe (secretary), Roger Sermersheim and Lincoln Edwards {eg_agenda_oct}{eg_board}. Members are elected from numbered districts; county results show Districts 1, 3 and 5 on the 2018 and 2022 ballots, District 2 in 2020 and 2024 and District 4 in 2020 {gc_2018}{gc_2022}{gc_2020}{gc_2024}. The Daily Clarion describes the 2026 seats as District 1 (Barton Township), District 3 (Oakland City) and District 5 (at-large) {pdc_filing}.

Seats on the 2026 ballot: three seats, each electing one member, matching the state list {pdc_filing}{in_list}. All three current holders are running again: Sevier, elected unopposed in District 1 in 2018 and 2022, faces Joshua Hugh Maikranz; Brewer, who won District 3 in 2022 by one vote (162 to 161 over Orbie Day, with Rebecca S. Frederick third in the precinct totals summed by this guide), is unopposed; and Rowe, who won the District 5 at-large seat in 2022 over incumbent Steven Schenks (945 to 683, summed precinct totals), is unopposed {gc_2018}{gc_2022}{pdc_slates}.

Budget and SEA 1 (2026): Galvin told the board June 8, 2026 that SEA 1 will cost the district about $400,000 over three years but that budgeting and the closing of Francisco Elementary let the district absorb the loss, saying 'We are very far from closing our doors' {pdc_sb1}. The board approved a 2027 budget in August that Galvin said is 'very near what it was last year,' and the October 13, 2026 agenda lists final approval of the 2027 budget {pdc_facilities}{eg_agenda_oct}.

Textbooks and insurance (July 2026): Galvin said the end of state textbook reimbursement, while the ban on textbook fees remains, leaves the district paying about $250,000 for K–8 textbooks; the board also approved a new employee health insurance bid that is still more than $12,000 above the prior year {pdc_textbook}.

Custodial outsourcing (January–May 2026): citing state funding cuts and SEA 1, the board sought bids to contract out custodial work; union members and supporters urged the board to keep the unionized staff {pdc_custodial_jan}{pdc_janitorial_feb}. After bids ranging from $484,584 to $948,682, compared with about $515,691 now spent, the board decided April 13 to keep its custodians, and approved a contract with them May 11 running through June 2030 {pdc_union_apr}{pdc_union_may}.

Enrollment and school choice: in his January 2026 State of the Schools report Galvin called enrollment a main challenge, reporting that 195 students who live in the district attend school elsewhere while 47 come in from outside, and that state dollars tied to enrollment are down more than $2 million over a decade {pdc_state}.

Consolidation: Galvin told the board in April 2026 that 'The state is moving and pushing towards consolidation,' citing a bill directing the Department of Education to evaluate school corporations, and said in June that the only way the district would close is if legislators forced consolidation {pdc_union_apr}{pdc_sb1}.

Facilities: the board approved up to $232,150 for new gym bleachers in March 2026, hired a firm in May to do a $15,000 facilities audit of all buildings, and is holding off on some projects until the audit is done {pdc_bleachers}{pdc_union_may}{pdc_facilities}. The 2027 capital projects plan lists roofing, flooring and parking lot projects and rooftop HVAC units {eg_capital}. In August the board bought a 0.16-acre lot across from campus for parking for $15,000 from board member Lincoln Edwards, who abstained; Sevier said Edwards had bought and cleared the burned property so the school could acquire it for what he had put into it {pdc_facilities}.

Safety and policies: in February 2026 the board unanimously approved a visitor management system that checks visitors against the sex offender registry, an anonymous reporting system, new defibrillators and classroom bleeding-control kits {pdc_safety}. For 2026–27 the district barred student cell phones for the full day, including lunch, and ended suspensions for excessive tardies {pdc_sb1}.

Academics and programs (2026): the board adopted McGraw Hill reading (Wonders) for elementary grades and StudySync for middle school language arts, started a construction trades program, and planned a free dual-credit 'College Core' pilot with Indiana University {pdc_union_apr}{pdc_union_may}{pdc_construction}{pdc_sb1}.
Board pay: in February 2026 the board raised member stipends from $2,000 to $4,500 a year, the first increase in at least 25 years; Rowe cast the only no vote {pdc_janitorial_feb}.
Forums: this guide found no 2026 candidate forum, questionnaire or campaign coverage for this race.
